annotations.annotation_text: Issy/daughter figure "Izzy" on page 257 ("The Mime of Mick, Nick and the Maggies"): the narcissistic mirror-daughter, modeled on Isolde and Swift's dual muses Stella and Vanessa, appears here within the children's games and pantomime on the green, Chuff vs. Glugg, the twenty-eight Rainbow Girls, the Angelus bell. Her prismatic splitting into twenty-eight Rainbow Girls reflects the cycle's Age of Heroes phase through youthful seduction and self-reflection.

annotations.annotation_text: Swiftian presence "stella" on page 257 ("The Mime of Mick, Nick and the Maggies"): the Dean of St. Patrick's Cathedral haunts this passage within the children's games and pantomime on the green, Chuff vs. Glugg, the twenty-eight Rainbow Girls, the Angelus bell. His dual lovers Stella and Vanessa mirror Issy's split personalities, while his savage satire infuses the Age of Heroes dream with political and scatological ferocity.
sources: Ehrenpreis, Irvin. Swift: The Man, His Works, and the Age. https://archive.org/details/swiftmanhisworks01ehre

annotations.annotation_text: Polysyllabic thunderclap on page 257 ("The Mime of Mick, Nick and the Maggies"): one of ten 100-letter words synthesizing thunder across world languages, signaling a Viconian cataclysm within the children's games and pantomime on the green, Chuff vs. Glugg, the twenty-eight Rainbow Girls, the Angelus bell. This divine acoustic blast — fusing Hindi, Greek, Latin, French, Italian, Irish, and Norse roots — marks a civilizational transition in the Age of Heroes phase.
sources: Vico, Giambattista. Scienza Nuova (On the Thunder). https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/vico/
Atherton, James S. The Books at the Wake. https://archive.org/details/booksatwake0000athe
